A pre-grant, not a ceiling

PR playground for #4008. The report was right that something is wrong, and wrong about what.

The correction that changes the fix

#4008 says 33 skills are "unable to carry out their own instructions". That framing is false. From the Claude Code docs, verbatim:

The allowed-tools field grants permission for the listed tools during the turn that invokes the skill, so Claude can use them without prompting you for approval. It does not restrict which tools are available: every tool remains callable, and your permission settings still govern tools that are not listed.

It is a pre-grant. An agent's tools: is a ceiling; a skill's allowed-tools is not. Nothing is blocked, and no skill silently reports work it never did.

Three real consequences survive the correction

  • A missing pre-grant puts an approval prompt in the middle of the skill's own procedure. Avoiding that is the field's entire purpose.
  • The Cursor host reads the same field off the generated command files and treats it as a hard ceiling. Same text, stricter reading, real breakage.
  • Prose honesty. A skill that reads as if it performs work it was never equipped to perform misleads the next author, whatever the runtime does.

Why the count is 11, not 33

The checker counts only imperative instruction lines and strips fenced code blocks first. A pattern skill quoting a command is teaching, not instructing, and that distinction is the whole judgment call in the issue. A gate that flagged every fenced block would report most of the corpus and be ignored, which is worse than one that reports less and is believed.

Two false positives were caught on the first run and removed: cleanup_expired() is a Python function and --lf is a pytest flag. Neither is a shell command. Tightening for those then dropped four true positives (agent-browser, style-dictionary) because the pattern excluded hyphens, so the final rule allows hyphens inside the command word while still rejecting a leading flag.

Nine narrow, two widen

The ratio is itself the finding: these are mostly reference skills whose prose drifted into the imperative, not skills that were under-equipped.

SkillCallWhy
configureWIDEN, doneAn interactive settings wizard. Editing config is the job. Added Edit, Write.
testing-e2eNARROW, donecontext: fork + agent: test-generator. The agent writes tests; the skill teaches.
doctorWIDENAlready carries Bash. A skill trusted to run commands should not prompt to drop a debug file.
7 othersNARROWReference and rules docs describing what a gate, layer, or CLI does.

The gate is proven to fail, both ways

=== FAULT ARM 1: a NEW offender must turn the gate red ===
  OK: gate went red
=== FAULT ARM 2: a STALE baseline entry must turn the gate red ===
  OK: gate went red
=== restored ===
allowed-tools check: 9 known offender(s), 0 new, 0 stale (baseline 9)

The second arm is the one that keeps the baseline a ratchet instead of a permanent amnesty: an entry that stops offending must be deleted, or the gate fails.

Run it

node scripts/allowed-tools-check.mjs --report
node scripts/allowed-tools-check.mjs
docs/skills-allowed-tools-direction.md carries the per-skill call for all eleven, and is the brief for the remaining mechanical edits. src/skills/CONTRIBUTING-SKILLS.md said "Restrict tools when active", which the docs above disprove; it is corrected in the same change.
